evidence: src/application/get-order-use-case.ts: `async execute(orderId: string, request?: Request): Promise<OrderDto>`: the use-case contract takes an Express HTTP Request, which is a transport/framework concern that belongs to infrastructure (controller).
The `request` parameter is never used in the method body. The real work (findById, NotFoundError, toOrderDto) is valid application orchestration.

Graph: OrderController@src/infrastructure/order-controller.ts injects GetOrderUseCase, so the infrastructure controller is where the Request should be handled and turned into plain inputs such as orderId.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Most of GetOrderUseCase fits the application layer. It loads the order through the domain OrderRepository port, throws a domain NotFoundError when nothing is found, and maps the result to an application DTO. That is normal use-case orchestration. The problem is the public method signature: `execute(orderId: string, request?: Request)` takes an Express HTTP Request. That puts a transport and framework concern, which belongs to the infrastructure layer (the presentation/controller side), into the use case's contract. A use case should not depend on how it is called. The parameter is optional and unused, so the file holds no actual HTTP-handling logic, which is why confidence is moderate. Even so, it exposes HTTP request handling as part of the use case's interface, and that belongs in OrderController in infrastructure. The bare `import { Request } from "express"` is an import-direction question, which is out of scope. This finding is about the method's contract only.
